messages.author: 21a7c1b5edb3112d
messages.subject: FFI interop and gcc-bridge
parts:
Hi all; especially Alex

Out of boredem, out of the desire for a challenge I have been messing about with the idea of implementing a system for getting full FFI working in R, including supporting the API surface (or as much as possible) for R extensions. My current ideas for an approach is to have a user configurable setup where it trys to do FFI through a selectable one of nestedVM, JNF / libffi / JNI cruft, rserver magics.

I noticed that, as I was building out the C api surface and some test cases that gcc-bridge has appeared; it looks like an interesting approach but I would like to know more about what the ideas are behind it.

- Do we forsee it as the sole solution to C / Fortran interop (I dont think that is perhaps the best idea as I can see people having R extensions that are complex and linked to many many things)
- Are there thoughts on supporting LLVM as well as GCC's gimple ?
- Whats the performance like on it ?
- Do you guys think that an approach that can offer different FFI implementations is a good thing, or plain insane ?

-- Greg

messages.author: f06db63329fab1f9
messages.subject: Re: FFI interop and gcc-bridge
parts:
Dear Greg,

First, AWESOME! So glad you're looking at this.

I think there will be many cases where there will be no other option for a foreign library than for Renjin to invoke a native library, whether because of complex dependencies or performance concerns. Building out a drop-in replacement for the R headers and (some) API calls seems like the best way to go. Take a look at github.com/twall/jna : I think I've already started to incorporate this into Renjin's code base: it's a nice library that allows you to load and invoke native libraries dynamically, so it should be easier than generating JNI cruft. 

gcc-bridge is rather more experimental, but i think there will be some bigger payoffs down the road: primarily because it opens the door to dynamically rewriting existing C/Fortran code to operate on Renjin vector interfaces rather than arrays, and so operate on data larger than can fit in memory.

The performance seems rather good -- by using the Gimple as input, it's easy to tell which values need to be addressable and which don't, so you can avoid the traditional C-to-Java approach of sticking everything into a big array: most variables don't need to be addressable and can be allocated on Java's stack or heap at worst. So on the whole the resulting code runs about the same as if you would translate the C to Java by hand. (maybe better, because our gimple input has already been optimized by gcc)

Right now, I've been working exclusive to process Gimple rather than say LLVM IR because I'm a bit more familiar with GCC and because I believe it's generally what's used to compile R packages, so we don't have to touch the makefiles, compiler flags, etc, or deal with compiler quirks.

The wall that i've hit with gcc-bridge at present is that the gimple output from GCC is meant for debugging purposes and in some cases is not complete. I'm trying to compile the appl library, for example, and GCC spits out "constant nodes" all over the place without giving us the value of the constant! I've started to write a GCC plugin that can dump precisely what we need, but I'm feeling my way through the GCC internals at a rather slow pace.

As I said above, I think there will still be plenty of cases where renjin simply needs to call a native library, and far from insane, I think it's quite doable. Particularly in the cases where the package is written using .C and .Fortran calling interface. Handling the .Call interface and callbacks into R will be trickier, but possible in many cases. I would warn you away from NestedVM-- it's not particularly amenable to dynamic loading (see my first attempt at renjin via nestedvm: http://code.google.com/p/r4jvm/) but otherwise you're probably on the right track.

So please! Experiment away, and share your results, even if they're half-finished. I've been resisting a move to github for the project because I feel a little bad for google code and all it's project pages adorned with "moved to github" notices, but if SVN is keeping people from forking and sharing their code than we should move quick!

Best,

Alex
